## 2

You don’t have to trust space photos to check the Earth’s shape. Long before spaceflight, people noticed that different stars are visible at different latitudes and that Earth casts a curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses. You can also compare the Sun’s angle at noon with someone far north or south of you; those measurements fit a curved surface.

The evidence consistently supports a roughly spherical Earth. What convinced you it was flat, and what kind of observation would make you reconsider?

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it’s a mixture of colors. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, it meets tiny molecules of air that scatter some of that light in different directions.

Here’s the important part: blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, and air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths much more strongly. So when you look at the sky away from the Sun, blue light is reaching your eyes from all across it.

Why not violet, which has an even shorter wavelength? Sunlight contains less violet, and our eyes are much less sensitive to it.

At sunset, sunlight travels through a longer stretch of atmosphere. Much of the blue gets scattered out of the direct beam before it reaches you, leaving more reds and oranges.
